paras: The attempted lynching of Woodson Towns was a mob's effort in Memphis, Tennessee, in the spring of 1919 to seize Towns, a Black street car passenger who had been wounded after a conductor was shot. Sheriff Oliver Hazard Perry turned the mob away at the county jail, and the Chicago Defender reported that there was neither a riot nor a lynching.

According to a Century News Service account, a street car conductor on the Florida line in South Memphis was shot and killed, on May 11 in one reading of the text. The Defender stated that nobody knew who shot him. The motorman then picked up the gun the conductor had dropped and fired on two Black passengers, Woodson Towns and Elijah Stackhouse, whom the report described as unarmed; both were wounded.

Towns, also spelled Townes, was taken to a hospital, where a mob of about 200 came looking for him. The crowd went next to the police station, where a police captain let it search the cells, and then gathered in front of the county jail and demanded 'the body of Towns'. There Sheriff Perry, surrounded by his deputies, took out his watch and gave the mob ten minutes to disperse, and when its members threatened the jail he invited any who felt that way to come in. No one accepted, and the deputies arrested men carrying concealed weapons, among them two conductors who were jailed.

Talk then spread that Black Memphis would be 'cleaned out' on a Saturday night, and residents of Beale Street and South Memphis, saying they had no protection from the city, prepared to defend their homes.

The Defender reported that no true bill had been found against Townes and that none was likely, and that Towns was out on bond. It credited a Black Memphis leader with counseling both sides, and wrote that Black Memphis was determined to prevent another lynching and burning in the city. No report on the conductor's killer or on Stackhouse's case appears in the coverage.

The episode appears only in the Chicago Defender of June 7, 1919, where a long Century News Service story ran on page 17 under the headline 'Memphis Sheriff Stops Big Riot', with subheads such as 'Mob Visit Hospital', 'Perry Faces Them', 'White Memphis Aroused' and 'Towns Out on Bonds'. The story praised Sheriff Perry as a 'strong man' before whom mobs dispersed and wrote that white Memphis had 'woke up' and that newspaper agitation had given way to 'an appeal to sense'. It placed the blame on the Memphis Street Railway Company for hiring recent arrivals from rural Mississippi, Alabama and Arkansas, and on the white newspapers and the 'silence of the white churches'. The text survives only in heavily garbled OCR, printed twice with differing readings of names and datelines.

Although the story first says no one knew who shot the conductor, a garbled later passage calls him the mob's comrade, 'the man they had killed in the attempt to take the life of a wounded, defenseless, innocent man'. One corrupted line also says the mob 'had Townes tied in a rope to the tree', but the same story reports that the mob was turned away, that there was 'no lynching', and that Towns was later free on bond.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Woodson Towns
bases: A mob of about 200 went to a hospital, the police station and the county jail seeking the wounded Townes and demanded 'the body of Towns' before the sheriff dispersed it (A3), an attempted lynching.

A mob of about 200 sought to seize and kill Townes after a conductor's shooting, but Sheriff Perry turned it away and Towns was later out on bond (A3, A7); the Defender states there was 'no lynching' (A6), so no one was killed by the mob.
All coverage is one Century News Service story printed in a single Chicago Defender issue (A2-A7); no second, independent report was found.

accounts.label: Black correspondent (Century News Service)
accounts.gist: A conductor was shot by an unknown person, and the motorman turned the gun on two unarmed Black passengers; a mob of conductors and others sought the wounded Townes until Sheriff Perry faced it down, and there was no riot and no lynching.

framing.detail: The Defender's 'Memphis Sheriff Stops Big Riot' praised Sheriff Perry, called Towns and Stackhouse unarmed and the mob's target 'innocent', and blamed the Street Railway Company, the white newspapers and the 'silence of the white churches'.

versions.value: A garbled passage refers to 'their comrade, the man they had killed in the attempt to take the life of a wounded, defenseless, innocent man', which may attribute his death to his own side.

conflicts.note: Both come from the same story; the second passage is too corrupt to read as a firm claim.

conflicts.field: what the mob did to Townes

versions.value: One OCR passage says 'the cavaliers already had Townes tied in a rope to the tree'.
The same story says the mob was turned away, there was 'no lynching', and Towns was out on bond.

conflicts.note: The rope passage is badly garbled and sits beside text saying the mob was stopped; the later, clearer statements are better evidence.

record_check.dossier: Woodson Towns and Elijah Stackhouse, both wounded by the motorman; the mob sought Towns.
Shooting/wounding of two Black men and a mob threat; no Black person was killed. The only death was the conductor's, by an unknown shooter.
1 (the street car conductor), not a victim of the mob.
Townes was in a hospital and then held by the authorities; the mob tried to take him from custody.
A mob of about 200 described as the conductor's comrades; two conductors jailed; the motorman fired the shots.
Shooting dated May 11 (OCR); mob visit soon after; reported June 7, 1919.
Townes faced an illegible charge, apparently connected with the conductor's death; no true bill found.

record_check.record: garbled text, man freed from fire, grand jury declined true bill
record_check.dossier: A conductor was shot; the motorman wounded two Black passengers; a mob sought Townes at the hospital, station and jail; Sheriff Perry dispersed it; no lynching; Towns out on bond.

info: The conductor's shooting is dated May 11 in one OCR version; the datelines read June 8 and June 14 in an issue dated June 7, so the mob's visit falls between May 11 and early June 1919.
On a street car on the Florida line in South Memphis; the mob went to a hospital, the police station and the county jail.
Woodson Towns (also 'Townes'; OCR 'Towne Towner') and Elijah Stackhouse, two Black passengers wounded by the motorman; the mob then sought Townes.
Townes apparently faced a charge connected with the conductor's death; the charge is not legible, but the Defender reports no true bill had been found against him.
The motorman (OCR 'N.W. Booker' / 'M. W. Tucker') shot the two passengers; a mob described as avenging 'their comrade' sought Townes; two conductors were jailed.
The mob dispersed; Towns was out on bond.

sources.note: Century News Service story 'Memphis Sheriff Stops Big Riot': conductor shot by unknown person; motorman turns gun on two Black passengers, Woodson Towns and Elijah Stackhouse, wounding both.
quotes: Who shot him nobody knows. Perhaps no one ever will know.
They were Woodson Towns and Elijah Stackhouse. They were unarmed, of course. Both men were wounded.

sources.note: Continuation, 'Mob Visit Hospital', 'Perry Faces Them', 'Two Jailed': mob of about 200 seeks Townes at hospital, police station and county jail; Sheriff Perry disperses it and two conductors are jailed.
quotes: The mob dispersed, as all mobs will do before a strong man.

sources.note: Continuation, 'Threats Against All': talk of cleaning out Black Memphis on Saturday night; Beale Street and South Memphis prepare to defend their homes.
quotes: They knew that thus far they have not enjoyed the protection of their government.

sources.note: Continuation, 'White Memphis Aroused': the law became active, newspaper talk gave way to an appeal to sense; 'There was no riot.' Interleaved with advertisements.
quotes: The big and loose talk in the newspapers was succeeded by an appeal to sense

sources.note: Continuation: 'no lynching'; no true bill found against Townes; blames the Memphis Street Railway Company's hiring of recent rural migrants.

set_aside: Editorial on Villard's charge that Tennessee lynched a Black soldier and the Memphis Commercial-Appeal's denial; nothing on Towns or the street car shooting.
